analysis.one_liner: Requires taxpayers earning over $1 million a year to pay at least 30% of their income in federal taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill, requiring millionaires to pay at least a 30% effective tax rate, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never advanced before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill created a "fair share" minimum tax: anyone with adjusted gross income above $1 million would pay at least 30% of their income (after allowing charitable deductions) in combined federal taxes, closing the gap that lets some millionaires pay lower effective rates than ordinary workers. It counted income from all sources, and the $1 million threshold would rise with inflation. It never received a committee hearing, a markup, or a floor vote in either chamber, and expired when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers earning under $1 million, whose taxes would not rise at all under the bill. The federal deficit would shrink by billions per year according to the bill's own statement, reducing pressure for future tax increases or spending cuts that fall on everyone else. Middle-class workers who feel it is unfair to pay a higher effective rate than millionaires would see that gap closed by law.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a minimum effective tax rate of 30% on adjusted gross income above $1 million, so millionaires can no longer pay a lower effective rate than middle-class families.

Collects the difference between the 30% minimum and what the taxpayer currently pays in regular tax, alternative minimum tax, and payroll taxes, meaning the tax targets only those whose rate falls below 30%.
Per the bill's own statement of purpose, would 'cut the deficit by billions of dollars a year' without raising taxes on anyone earning under $1 million.

analysis.who_pays: Households earning over $1 million in adjusted gross income, who would pay the difference between their current tax bill and a 30% minimum effective rate. Charitable deductions would still reduce the new tax, softening the cost for the largest givers.

drawbacks.text: The bill explicitly allows high-income taxpayers to reduce the new tax by charitable contributions, which preserves a large deduction for exactly the wealthy households it targets.

Because it is structured as a minimum tax on top of the existing system, the underlying deductions and loopholes that let millionaires pay low rates remain on the books; the bill itself describes the provision as an 'interim step' and a 'floor' rather than structural reform.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On its merits, the bill would have raised substantial revenue from the roughly 0.1% of households earning over $1 million per year, with no direct cost to anyone else — the main cost being higher taxes on high earners and, opponents would argue, possible drag on investment. Its design was sound in principle (a floor, not a confiscatory rate, and it preserves charitable giving). The real weakness is that it was introduced as a message bill in a Senate where the majority did not bring it to any committee action, so its substantive merits were never seriously tested.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and the Congress ended with no committee action, no debate, and no vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on April 27, 2017.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, the standard first step for tax legislation.
The Finance Committee took no action on the bill: no hearing, no markup, no vote, and it never reached the Senate floor.
The 115th Congress ended in January 2019 without the bill advancing, meaning it died in committee.
The bill had 16 Democratic cosponsors, all 17 total sponsors being Democrats, and no Republican support.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households earning over $1 million per year are better off, since they continue to pay effective tax rates that can fall below 30% after deductions. Tax-planning industries that help high earners minimize taxes also keep the status quo.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High-income households and their tax advisors

for.name: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to impose a 30% minimum effective tax rate on taxpayers earning over $1 million.

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren and 15 other Democratic senators
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as original cosponsors, giving it a full slate of Democratic support but no Republican cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Senate committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral and took no action: no hearing, no markup, and no vote during the entire 115th Congress.

against.name: Senate Republican majority
against.what_they_did: Committee leadership made no move to advance the bill; the majority chose not to schedule it for committee consideration or floor action, which in practice kept a tax increase on high earners off the agenda.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 senators behind the bill were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored it, and with Republicans controlling both the Finance Committee and the Senate, the bill had no path forward.

industries.industry: High-income households earning over $1 million per year
industries.note: The bill's entire purpose is to raise their effective tax rate to a 30% floor, ending the situation where millionaires can pay lower rates than middle-income workers. It allows a modified charitable deduction, so the tax is somewhat reduced for large charitable givers.

industries.industry: Tax-sheltered investment and fund industries (hedge funds, private equity, real estate partnerships)
industries.note: These industries specialize in converting compensation into capital gains and other low-taxed forms of income; a 30% minimum rate directly reduces the value of that structuring. Their clients would pay more.
